title: The bar at the mouth
teaches: Where the Columbia meets the Pacific swell, and why the bar is one of the most dangerous in the world
summary: **The bar is where the river's sand meets the sea.** The Columbia drops its load where its outflow slows in the ocean, and swell and storms shove the sand back into a shifting arc of shoals across the mouth.
**The ebb makes the waves worse.** Swell running into the outgoing current slows, shortens and grows taller, because its energy arrives faster than it can move on.
**A wave breaks at about a seventh.** Once a wave's height reaches about a seventh of its length it can no longer hold its shape, and on the bar the biggest waves of a swell reach that first.

**The same swell can be safe at one hour and breaking at another.** Over a tide the current swings from flood to ebb, so the bar is kindest near the end of the flood and worst at the height of the ebb.
**A spring freshet strengthens the ebb.** More river water running out means a stronger current against the swell.
**The jetties squeezed the ebb into one channel.** Built from 1885 to 1917 and in 1939, they scoured a deeper, steadier channel, and dredges keep it deep.
**Pilots and lifeboat crews read the bar for a living.** Bar pilots take every large ship across, and the Coast Guard trains its surf crews at Cape Disappointment.

blocks.text: In August 1775 the Spanish navigator Bruno de Heceta, sailing north along the coast, found a bay where the current ran so strongly out to sea that he could barely hold his ship in it. He judged it the mouth of a great river. His crew was too weak with scurvy to work the ship across the breakers, and he sailed on. In the spring of 1792 George Vancouver's ships passed the same line of breakers and went on north to the Strait and Puget Sound.

On 11 May 1792 the American trader Robert Gray, in the *Columbia Rediviva*, waited for his moment and took his ship through the breakers into fresh water. He named the river after his ship. Gray had found a gap that was open when he crossed, and the bar has been closing and opening ever since. In July 1841 the US Navy's *Peacock*, part of Charles Wilkes's survey of the coast and the Sound, ran aground on the shoal north of the entrance and broke up; no one died, and the shoal has been Peacock Spit ever since. Counts of the ships lost on and around the bar since run to the thousands, though no one kept a full list, and the stretch of coast is called the Graveyard of the Pacific.
The bar's danger comes and goes on a timetable. The same swell from the same storm can roll across it in long, low hills at one hour and stand up in breaking walls six hours later.

Lesson 7 showed that a wave carries energy, not water, and that its energy travels at a definite speed for its period and the depth beneath it. Swell from a distant storm arrives at the Columbia's mouth with a period of ten seconds or more, the long, regular waves of open ocean.

Twice a day the tide floods in through the mouth and twice a day it ebbs out, and on the ebb the whole outflow of the Columbia rides out with it. The river's fresh water is lighter than seawater and spreads out over the top, so at the surface, where the waves are, the ebb runs especially hard. Swell running into that current is in water moving the wrong way. The waves keep the same period, a crest every ten seconds or so, but each crest makes less headway, so they crowd together: they get shorter. Their energy is still arriving from the ocean at the old rate, but it can no longer move on as fast, so it piles up in each wave, and the waves get taller.[^action] A strong enough ebb stops short waves altogether.[^blocking]

Taller and shorter means steeper. A wave can only get so steep: once its height reaches about a seventh of its length, the crest outruns the water beneath it and topples, and the wave breaks. Over the bar the water is also shallow, which slows and steepens the waves further, as lesson 7's waves slow in shallow water. The waves in a swell are not all the same size, either, and the biggest in a set can be nearly twice the height a forecast gives. They are the ones that break first.[^biggest]

The swell's period is 10 seconds, the bar 12 m deep; heights are the significant heights a forecast gives.

blocks.text: So the best time to cross is near the end of the flood or at high slack, when the current is weak or running in with the waves, and the worst is the height of the ebb. In late spring the freshet of lesson C1 adds the snowmelt of half a continent to every ebb, and in winter, when the river is lower, the swell is at its biggest. Small boats and fishers who use the bar plan their crossings on the tide table as much as the forecast.

Lesson 4 showed that a river drops what it carries when it slows. The Columbia carries sand down to its mouth, and where its outflow fans out into the ocean and slows, the sand settles. The swell pushes it back toward land, and storms shift it north and south along the coast. Between the river pushing out and the sea pushing in, the sand builds a broad arc of shoals across the mouth: the **bar**. Oceanographers call such a shape an ebb-tidal delta.

blocks.caption: The mouth of the Columbia from above: the jetties, the shoals beside them, the dredged channel and the bar beyond it. A sketch, not a chart.

blocks.text: Before the jetties, the bar had no fixed gap. The river's outflow found one channel across it for a few years, then another, sometimes north near Cape Disappointment, sometimes south toward Clatsop Spit, and in places the water over the bar was no deeper than about 6 m (20 feet) at low tide. A channel that was safe last season could be a shoal this one, which is why ships waited outside for days for a captain who knew this year's bar.

From 1885 the Army Corps of Engineers built a **jetty**, a wall of rock several kilometres long, out from the south shore, and later another from the north. A jetty works on the river's current: it squeezes the ebb into one channel, and the faster current scours that channel deeper and keeps it in one place. Within a few decades the bar channel was far deeper than it had been, and it stopped wandering.

blocks.caption: Taming the bar. Dates of the jetties from the Corps of Engineers' histories, rounded to the year.

blocks.text: The jetties also caught sand. The sand moving along the coast piled up against them, and the beaches beside them grew out to sea: Clatsop Spit on the Oregon side and the shore under Peacock Spit on the Washington side. Dredges still work the channel every year, and the Corps has rebuilt the jetties' ends more than once as storms knock the rock down.[^dredge]
None of this made the bar calm. A deeper channel gives a wave more room before it trips on the bottom, but the ebb is as strong as ever, and squeezed between the jetties it is stronger.

Every large ship that crosses the bar has a **bar pilot** aboard, a mariner licensed to take ships across this one piece of water, who knows its channel, its currents and how it behaves in every sea. Pilots have worked the bar since the 1840s. They meet ships offshore and climb aboard from a pilot boat by rope ladder, or in rough weather are lowered to the deck from a helicopter, then take the ship in to Astoria, where river pilots take over.

Small boats rely on the Coast Guard, which closes the bar to small craft when the breakers make it too dangerous and sends lifeboats out to those caught on it. The Coast Guard's school for motor lifeboat crews is at Cape Disappointment, on the north side of the mouth, because the bar offers surf to train in through most of the year.

blocks.title: Outdoors: watch the bar on an ebb
points: Pick a winter day with a big swell forecast, and find the time of high water at the river mouth in a tide table.
Watch from the North Head or Cape Disappointment side in Washington, or from the viewing platform by the South Jetty in Fort Stevens State Park in Oregon.
Note the breakers over the bar near high slack, then watch again two or three hours into the ebb. Look for the lines of white water thickening and spreading across the channel as the current builds.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the Columbia bar
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: With the same swell offshore, why are the waves on the Columbia bar steeper on the ebb than on the flood?
choices: Running into the outgoing current, the waves shorten and grow taller as their energy bunches up
On the ebb the water over the bar is deeper, and deeper water lets waves grow larger
The ebb carries river sand that thickens the water and lifts the waves higher
items.why: The waves keep their period but make less headway against the current, so they crowd closer. Energy still arriving from the ocean piles into each wave, so they get taller as well as shorter.

items.ask: About how steep can a wave get before it breaks?
choices: Its height can reach about a seventh of its length
Its height can reach the depth of the water beneath it
Its height can reach about half of its length
items.why: Steeper than about one in seven, a crest outruns the water beneath it and topples. In shallow water waves break sooner, at a height near the depth.

items.ask: Why does the Columbia bar shift from year to year?
choices: The river drops sand where its outflow slows at sea, and swell and storms push it back and along the coast
Earthquakes off the coast raise and lower the seabed a little every year
Ships' propellers stir up sand from the channel and pile it into new banks beside it
items.why: The bar is an ebb-tidal delta, built where river and sea push against each other. Before the jetties its channel wandered between the north and south sides of the mouth.

items.ask: What did the jetties built at the mouth from 1885 onward do?
choices: Squeezed the ebb into one channel, which scoured it deeper and held it in place
Blocked the swell so that waves no longer break over the bar
Stopped the river carrying sand to the sea, so the bar washed away
items.why: A jetty works on the current: the faster ebb between the jetties keeps one deep channel open. The swell still meets the ebb, so the bar still breaks.

items.ask: A small boat inside the Columbia's mouth waits for a winter swell to cross the bar. When is the best time to go?
choices: Near the end of the flood or at high slack, before the ebb begins
At the height of the ebb, while the current carries the boat out fastest
At low slack, when the water over the bar is at its shallowest
items.why: With the current weak or running in with the waves, the swell stays long and low. At the height of the ebb the same swell is shortest, tallest and most likely to break.

items.ask: Why does a big spring freshet make the bar more dangerous?
choices: More river water running out strengthens the ebb against the incoming swell
Snowmelt water is colder and denser than the sea, which makes waves steeper
The extra water raises the sea level at the mouth, and the swell grows with it
items.why: The ebb at the surface carries the river's outflow as well as the falling tide. A larger river means a stronger current for the swell to meet.

action.title: Wave action
action.text: Strictly, what a current conserves is not a wave's energy but its energy divided by its frequency relative to the moving water, which oceanographers call wave action. The figure's model keeps the wave action flux, with the waves' speed in water of the bar's depth, to find how tall they grow.

biggest.title: Significant wave height
biggest.text: Forecasts and buoys give the significant wave height, about the average of the highest third of the waves. In a few hundred waves, a few of them come near twice that height. The figure counts the bar as breaking once those biggest waves reach the breaking limit.

dredge.title: How deep is the channel?
dredge.text: The ship channel over the bar is dredged to about 17 m (55 feet), deeper than the river channel above it, to leave room for ships rising and falling in the swell. The sand dredged out is dumped at sea, and some of it is placed close to shore so it can feed the beaches.

blocking.title: When the ebb stops the waves
blocking.text: If the current against the waves runs at a quarter of the speed of deep-water waves, their energy can't make headway at all. The waves pile up where the current reaches that speed and break there. Short, choppy waves meet that limit first, so a strong ebb breaks the short waves where they stand and makes the long swell steeper.
